div.p: Introduction Drosophila melanogaster, a well-established model organism in biomedical research, has significantly advanced our understanding of genetic mechanisms underlying human diseases. Its genetic similarity to humans, with approximately 75% of human disease-related genes having orthologues in the fly genome, renders it a valuable tool for studying complex conditions like cancer. The organism's low cost, short life cycle, and manipulable genome make it ideal for highthroughput studies.
for the fight against cancer, as it helps inform researchers of the potential areas that require further research, especially with the rapid evolution of personalised medicine.

div.head: Main Text
div.p: Recent advances have enabled the use of Drosophila as a model for different cancer types, including colorectal, thyroid, lung, and brain cancers. These models replicate key tumor characteristics such as cell proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. Drosophila's utility in drug screening has been exemplified through heterochromatin-promoting assays and personalized medicine approaches using patient-specific gene expression data. Its role in testing therapeutic combinations, such as MEK inhibitors with statins for lung cancer, underscores its translational potential. Despite its utility, the model has notable limitations. Differences in tumor biology between flies and humans, especially regarding organ systems and immune responses, limit its applicability in certain cancer types and metastatic studies. Furthermore, environmental influences and the simplified genetic background of Drosophila may not accurately represent human cancer complexity. Ethical concerns and translational challenges also exist, warranting cautious interpretation of results. The recent advancements in CRISPR-based genome editing, particularly cytosine and adenine base editors, have improved gene-editing efficiency in Drosophila, supporting its ongoing use in precision oncology. Future directions point toward integrating Drosophila models with other in vivo and in silico systems to optimize personalized drug discovery and better emulate human tumor heterogeneity.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: While the use of Drosophila melanogaster has intrinsic limitations, its genetic tractability and compatibility with cutting-edge genomic tools position it as a complementary model to mammalian systems. Continued innovations in genetic engineering and model integration will further strengthen its role in translational oncology and precision medicine. This review explores the applications of the model in human cancer research and highlights the major challenges with its use. This is crucial

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Drosophila melanogaster is one of the most widely used model organisms in biomedical research. It belongs to the Drosophilidae family of flies, which are predominantly found around rotten or overripe fruits [1]. Many Drosophila species, especially the immigrans, the simulans, and the melanogaster, are now regarded as domestic species because of their close interactions with humans [2]. Drosophila melanogaster's use in genetic studies dates back over 100 years. e first experimental studies using Drosophila were conducted in 1906, while geneticists started using it in 1906 [3]. Over the years, scientists have been able to conduct not just descriptive, but also analytical studies on the organism. e completion of the human genome project was preceded by the completion of the Drosophila genome project in 2000. Comparisons of the two genome sequences revealed very close similarities, with up to 75% of human disease-causing genes having functional orthologues in the Drosophila genome. is makes it an excellent model for studying various human diseases [4].

Various other model organisms are used in biomedical research, including the mouse, Escherichia coli, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, yeast, Xenopus, etc. Studies involving these organisms help to advance the understanding of various disease processes, cellular mechanisms, structural development, etc. Apart from its genetic similarities with humans, Drosophila is an excellent model for several reasons: (i) its small size, (ii) ease of handling, (iii) inexpensiveness to maintain in the laboratory, (iv) having a short lifespan, (v) the ability to produce several offspring in a short time, (vi) the ability to express complex behavioural patterns, (vii) the low level of ethical concerns about its use in many countries, and (viii) its ease of genetic manipulation [3].

is review was based on a comprehensive literature search on databases such as PubMed, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect, using keywords such as "Drosophila melanogaster", "Drosophila cancer model", "Cancer research", "Fruit fly cancer model", etc. e review focuses on the application of Drosophila in cancer research, highlighting some of the recent advances and a few challenges in its use. is will contribute to our understanding of Drosophila biology and highlight areas for further studies on the organism's application in cancer research.

div.head: Fundamental biology and genetics of drosophila
div.p: Drosophila has a remarkable life cycle. It takes a single fly approximately 10 days to produce hundreds of offspring at standard room temperature.

is is a major advantage over the commonly used mouse models, which have a slower reproduction rate. e fly has four main developmental stages: embryo, larva, pupa and adult [5]. Following fertilisation, at standard temperature, the embryo develops in the egg for approximately one day and emerges as a larva. Over the next five days, the larva grows and moults three times before transitioning into the pupa. e adult fly emerges from the pupa after about four days of pupal metamorphosis [6]. Each of the fly stages has peculiar applications in biomedical studies. For instance, the embryo is often used for developmental biology studies, while the larva (especially at the third instar stage) is used for studies of developmental and physiological processes, and simple behavioural studies. e adult fly is a complex organism with structures that perform the corresponding functions of the brain, kidney, heart, lung, digestive and reproductive tracts, etc., in humans [5].

e organism is made up of the following groups of chromosomes: chromosome 1 or X (about 20% of the genome), autosomal chromosomes 2 and 3 (each about 40% of the genome), chromosome 4 (less than 1% of the chromosome), and chromosome Y (less than 1% of the genome). Female flies possess two X chromosomes while males have one X and one Y chromosome. Both genders possess two sets of the other groups of chromosomes. e X, Y and fourth chromosomes are acrocentric with a centromere dividing them into two arms, one longer than the other. Chromosomes 2 and 3, on the other hand, are metacentric, so the centromere is situated around the centre. Genetic markers are the visible traits that are used to identify each fly's genetic background. e most common markers are dominant, which are those that are visible in flies that possess only a copy of the mutation responsible for the trait. A recessive marker implies that the fly has two copies of the mutation responsible for the trait. e exceptions to this are the X-linked recessive markers, which are seen when the mutation occurs in males, since they possess only one copy of the X chromosome [3]. e genome is about 180 Mb in size, with about ⅔ occupied by the euchromatic region and the remaining ⅓ by the heterochromatic region. Following the first characterisation of the genome in 2000, its annotation has been revised several times, with a current release reporting a total sequence length of 143,726,002 bp. is contains 17,728 genes out of which 13,907 are protein coding while 3821 encode numerous noncoding RNA types. e functions of many of these genes and how they relate to humans are still being studied [7].

div.head: Applications of Drosophila in cancer research
div.p: e intricate genetic mutations driving tumorigenesis, tumor growth and metastasis highlight the need for simplified models to enhance our understanding of the involved genes, biochemical interactions and to evaluate strategies for inhibiting their effect with minimal toxicity. Drosophila being an excellent model organism finds great applications in screening compounds found to be profoundly useful in cancer therapy and treatment as a whole [8].

div.head: Application in cancer research
div.p: Historically, cancer studies have primarily relied on mammalian systems -from cell cultures to whole organisms. One of the Drosophila model's greatest early contributions came over two decades ago, when work in the fly's visual system unraveled the Ras signaling cascade. Approximately 40% of colorectal cancer (CRC) cases are characterized by KRAS mutations, rendering them insensitive to most CRC therapies [9]. Since most human cancers arise from epithelial tissues, researchers have now developed various Drosophila models that mimic epithelial-derived tumors. ese models not only display uncontrolled cell proliferation, but also exhibit key features of metastasis and invasion, making them strategically vital for translational discovery [5]. Drosophila serves as an excellent in vivo model for studying the clonal behavior of cells carrying oncogenic mutations. e mosaic methods allow researchers to label, observe and manipulate individual mutant cell clones within living tissues [9]. is has been instrumental in uncovering the molecular pathways that drive the progression of tumors toward malignancy.

div.head: Drosophila models in specific cancer types
div.p: e genetic similarity between Drosophila and humans enables the modeling of various cancer types in the fruit fly. Specific regions of Drosophila are engineered to mimic particular human cancers, reflecting shared genes and underlying biological mechanisms. Current Drosophila models have been developed for several cancer types, including colorectal, lung, thyroid, and brain cancers. Additionally, these models are used to investigate key molecular components involved in cancer, such as tumor suppressor genes, chromatin regulators, cell growth pathways, the tumor microenvironment, invasion, and metastasis [10].

div.head: D. melanogaster thyroid cancer model
div.p: yroid cancer involves diverse genetic mutations, notably in the RET receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK), a 120 kDa transmembrane protein implicated in both Drosophila and human thyroid cancers. Activating RET mutations are linked to multiple endocrine neoplasia types 2 A/2B (MEN2A/B) and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma (FMTC). To model these diseases, Drosophila genotypes such as GMR^dRetM559T and ptc^dRetM955T were engineered based on patient-derived RET^M918T mutations ([10]- [11]).

Researchers used the dRet^MEN2B Drosophila model to assess the efficacy of ZD6474 (vandetanib), developing a quantitative viability assay via the GAL4-UAS system. Targeting dRet^MEN2B in eye, wing, and leg tissues, they identified the patched promoter as key in oncogene-driven epithelial tumor formation. Structural optimization of ZD6474 using this model led to enhanced derivatives (AD57, AD58, AD80, AD81) with improved efficacy and reduced toxicity ([12]- [13]). Additional studies used Drosophila MTC models to explore novel drug targets and expand the chemical space beyond known inhibitors like sorafenib.

div.head: D. melanogaster lung cancer model
div.p: Lung cancer statistically holds the highest mortality rate among all cancer types. Conventional treatments typically involve chemoradiotherapy, often supplemented with targeted therapies. However, many current lung cancer drugs have demonstrated limited effectiveness in suppressing tumor growth and are associated with significant toxicity and the development of drug resistance [10]. Due to notable molecular and cellular similarities between the Drosophila tracheal system and vertebrate lung development, Drosophila melanogaster has become a valuable model for studying lung cancer. Using the GAL4/UAS system, Levine and Cagan (2016) developed a Drosophila lung cancer model featuring an oncogenic RAS^G12V mutation combined with PTEN knockdown (a negative regulator of the PI3K pathway). A chemical screen of 1,192 FDA-approved compounds-selected to reduce organismal lethality-identified two key drugs: trametinib, a MEK1/2 inhibitor, and fluvastatin, an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor commonly used to treat cardiovascular disease. ese compounds synergistically suppressed RAS and PI3K pathway activity, resulting in decreased cellular over proliferation, reduced systemic toxicity, and inhibition of A549 human non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell growth harboring the RAS^G12V mutation [10,14]. Trametinib remains the only MEK inhibitor currently FDA-approved for NSCLC treatment, either as a monotherapy or in combination with dabrafenib. Clinical use of this combination has shown improved patient survival and sustained therapeutic response.

div.head: D. melanogaster colorectal carcinoma model
div.p: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Its progression is driven by chromosomal abnormalities, genetic mutations, and epigenetic changes affecting genes involved in processes such as apoptosis, angiogenesis, cell proliferation, and differentiation. Key factors in CRC development include the activation of oncogenes like KRAS and BRAF, the loss of function in tumor suppressor genes such as APC, p53, DCC, and p16, as well as defects in DNA mismatch repair genes like MLH1 and MSH2 [10,15,16]. e genetic similarities between Drosophila and mammals enable effective modeling of colorectal cancer (CRC) in the fruit fly. ese models exhibit core characteristics of human CRC, including altered cellular differentiation, increased cell proliferation, and compromised intestinal homeostasis. Additionally, they provide a whole-organism platform to evaluate a range of CRC therapies. In a notable example, Bangi and colleagues (2016) successfully used Drosophila to model four to five common mutations found in CRC genotypes [15].

Drosophila studies reveal that tumor-associated senescent cells-arising from combined AKT, JNK, and DNA-damage signaling-promote intestinal tumorigenesis by recruiting macrophages and driving non-autonomous JNK activation, highlighting senescent cell-immune interactions as key contributors to colorectal epithelial transformation. Using patient-informed multigenic can generate emergent drug resistance (e.g., to PI3K inhibitors), enabling the discovery of an "induced dependence" strategy that identifies effective combinatorial therapies validated across fly, cell culture, xenograft, and mouse systems [17,18].

div.head: D. melanogaster glioma model
div.p: Adult gliomas are the most common primary brain tumors, and in Drosophila glioma model created by co-expressing constitutively active EGFR and PI3K in glial cells leads to excessive glial proliferation, brain enlargement, invasive behavior, and lethality at the third instar larval stage [19,20]. Introducing the human serotonin 5-HT7 receptor into this model reduced larval death, restored normal brain morphology in survivors, and supports its role as a tumor suppressor, findings that align with transcriptomic profiles from human glioblastomas [10].

div.head: D. melanogaster melanoma model
div.p: Drosophila melanogaster provides a powerful platform for melanoma research due to its conserved Ras/MAPK signaling architecture, enabling functional assessment and severity ranking of melanoma-associated mutations-such as those in MEK and other pathway components-and allowing rapid in vivo evaluation of mutation strength, tumorigenic potential, and drug responsiveness. is cross-species conservation makes Drosophila an efficient model for mechanistic studies and for developing mutationguided therapeutic strategies in melanoma [21].

div.head: D. melanogaster ovarian cancer model
div.p: Molecular processes in the Drosophila reproductive system mirror those involved in ovarian cancer metastasis. In fruit flies, for instance, follicular cells must undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to become border cells. As these border cells move toward the oocyte, they exhibit invasive properties that enable them to penetrate between nurse cells. ey also reorganize their intercellular junctions and modify their adhesion as they separate from the follicular epithelium. Because of these features, Drosophila border cells are considered a useful model for investigating ovarian cancer metastasis. Another similarity is that border cells migrate in clusters, much like ovarian cancer cells which form aggregates while suspended in malignant ascites [22].

div.head: D. melanogaster adenoid cystic carcinoma model
div.p: A Drosophila precision-medicine model of a patient's advanced adenoid cystic carcinoma enabled identification of a three-drug combination (vorinostat, pindolol, tofacitinib) that rescued lethality in vivo and produced a 12-month partial clinical response before resistance emerged, demonstrating the potential of fly-based screening to uncover therapeutic options for ACC [23].

div.head: Application in cancer drug screening and identification
div.p: Heterochromatin is a key regulator of chromosomal stability whose integrity is critical in preventing genomic instability and genomic instability and tumorigenesis, making it both a biomarker and a potential target in cancer prevention and therapy. A study developed a cost-effective in vivo method using Drosophila to identify compounds that promote heterochromatin formation, which could aid in cancer therapy. e DX1 Drosophila strain exhibits a variegated eye color phenotype, with the extent of red pigmentation inversely correlating to heterochromatin levels. In this screening method, eye variegation is quantified based on the surface area of red pigmentation occupying parts of the eye and is scored on a scale of 1 to 5. e screening method is straightforward and sensitive, allowing for testing compounds in vivo. Drug screening using this method provides a fast and inexpensive way of identifying heterochromatin-promoting drugs that could have beneficial effects in cancer therapeutics. Identifying compounds that promote the formation of heterochromatin could also lead to the discovery of epigenetic mechanisms of cancer development [8].

div.head: D. melanogaster personalized cancer therapy model
div.p: Personalized medicine seeks to tailor treatment to each individual patient, using the most effective drug to provide maximum therapeutic benefit while minimizing side effects. Understanding how genetics influence disease and affect drug toxicity and efficacy is crucial in personalized medicine. A major challenge lies in identifying which candidate genes have true therapeutic relevance. is task is made difficult by the intricate genetic interactions within a living organism. In this context, Drosophila serves as a valuable model for exploring these complex genetic relationships at the whole-organism level. To this effect two types of Drosophila models have been developed. e first is an in-silico Drosophila Patient Model (DPM), which simulates biomolecular regulation in cancer using patient-specific gene expression data to design personalized cancer treatment strategies. e second is an in vivo Drosophila Patient Model (DPM), where Drosophila is used in personalized cancer therapy through the creation of cancer avatars-flies that are genetically engineered to carry multiple mutations mirroring those found in human patients [10,24]. ese models help in drug screening and in identifying compounds with higher wholeorganism efficacy and decreased toxicity. One of the major challenges in personalized therapy, even when using multiple treatments, is the emergence of drug resistance. Identifying potential resistance early on is crucial for optimizing therapeutic strategies. Here, personalized Drosophila models prove valuable once again, as they have shown potential in helping to identify biomarkers associated with drug resistance.

div.head: Challenges and limitations of using Drosophila in cancer research
div.p: e use of Drosophila melanogaster in cancer research presents several challenges and limitations that must be acknowledged. While Drosophila offers unique advantages, such as genetic manipulability and the ability to model certain cancer hallmarks, significant differences in tumor biology compared to humans, limitations in modeling metastasis, and ethical concerns pose hurdles for translational research.

div.head: Differences in tumor biology
div.p: Drosophila and humans exhibit fundamental differences in tumor biology, which can limit the applicability of findings from fly models to human cancers. Drosophila lacks several mammalian organ systems, including mammary glands, prostate, and lungs, limiting direct modeling of cancers originating in these tissues.

Genetic Complexity: Human cancers are often characterized by a high degree of genetic heterogeneity, influenced by multiple mutations and environmental factors, which are difficult to replicate in Drosophila models [25]. Each tumor has its own unique profiling which in turn determines the rate of metastasis, degree of cachexia and their response to treatment [25].

Microenvironment: e tumor microenvironment plays a crucial role in cancer progression. Drosophila models may not fully capture the complexity of human stroma and immune interactions, especially because Drosophila's immune system lacks adaptive immunity and antibody-mediated responses that play crucial roles in human tumor immunology [26,27]. e fly's open circulatory system differs substantially from the closed human vascular system, complicating studies of tumorvasculature interactions and angiogenesis-dependent cancer progression [28].

div.head: Limitations in modeling metastasis
div.p: While Drosophila has been used to study tumor invasion and metastasis, there are inherent limitations. One of the most significant challenges involves modeling metastasis -a hallmark of advanced human cancers [29].

Metastatic Processes: e mechanisms of metastasis in Drosophila may not accurately reflect those in humans. While Drosophila models have been developed to study cell migration and invasion, they struggle to fully capture the complete metastatic cascade, including intravasation, circulation through bloodstream, extravasation, and colonization at distant sites [29,30]. Studies using RasV12 and DlgRNAi Drosophila cancer models demonstrate certain aspects of cancer progression, such as increased malignancy through chromosome aberrations and ROS accumulation [31].

Lack of Organ-Specific Models: Drosophila lacks certain organ systems present in humans including mammary glands, prostate, and lungs which can limit the direct modeling of cancers originating in these tissues and study of organ-specific metastasis and the systemic effects of cancer [28,32].

div.head: Genetic and environmental factors
div.p: e genetic background and environmental influences in Drosophila can also affect the outcomes of cancer studies. Drosophila models often utilize a simplified genetic background, which may not account for the multifactorial nature of human cancers [33]. Factors such as diet, lifestyle, and exposure to carcinogens, which significantly influence cancer development in humans, are not easily replicated in Drosophila [25].

div.head: Ethical concerns and translational limitations
div.p: Ethical considerations and the translational gap between Drosophila and human studies are significant challenges. e ethical concerns of the use of fruit fly, Drosophila melanogaster, in research are generally fewer compared to vertebrate animal models (like mice or monkeys), but they are not entirely non-existent [34].

e primary ethical considerations revolve around the evolving understanding of insect sentience and the application of ethical research principles. e applicability of animal warfare laws has been an issue of concern, giving that in most countries including under the U.S. Animals Welfare Act and the European Directive 2010/63/EU in the protection of animals used for scientific purposes, invertebrates like Drosophila are not classified as "animals" and are therefore explicitly excluded from the robust welfare regulations that cover vertebrates [35]. is exclusion means researchers are not legally required to adhere to the same strict housing, care, or institutional review standards applied to mammalian models [36]. e main ethical challenge stems from growing scientific evidence suggesting that insects, including Drosophila, may possess nociception (the detection of harmful stimuli) and potentially sentience (the ability to experience feelings, including pain) [37]. erefore in the precautionary principle, ethicists argue that until definitive proof of the absence of pain or suffering is established, researchers should apply a precautionary principle and afford some level of moral consideration to these beings [38].

While Drosophila research is generally considered ethical, the implications of findings for human health must be carefully considered, especially when translating results to clinical settings [24]. e differences in biological systems can lead to challenges in translating findings from Drosophila to human therapies, often resulting in a lack of successful clinical applications [21]. One of the most significant limitations of using Drosophila for translational cancer drug research is the difference in Pharmacokinetics (PK) and drug metabolism compared to humans. Drosophila is excellent for studying the conserved genetic pathways that drive cancer, however its distinct physiology makes it a poor model for predicting how a drug will be absorbed, distributed, metabolized, and excreted (ADME) in a human patient [39]. us, while Drosophila serves as a valuable model for certain aspects of cancer research, the differences in tumor biology which include the difference in pharmacokinetics (PK) and drug metabolism compared to humans, limitations in modeling metastasis, and ethical concerns highlight the need for caution in interpreting results. Future research may benefit from integrating findings from Drosophila with other model systems to enhance the understanding of cancer biology and improve therapeutic strategies.

div.head: Advancements in genetic manipulation and crispr technology in Drosophila
div.p: In recent years, the field of biotechnology has seen great advancement due to the progress made with genome-modifying enzymes, especially the CRISPR/Cas9 system [40]. Varieties of CRISPR adaptations have been made for different purposes. In the homology-directed repair (HDR) mechanism, a donor DNA template encoding the desired nucleotide substitution is supplied alongside the CRISPR/Cas9. e Cas9 creates the double-stranded breaks (DSBs) while the HDR uses the donor DNA as a repair template; by doing so, it installs the desired mutation, albeit at a very low efficiency [41,42]. Beyond the HDR mechanism, novelty approaches such as the CRISPR base editors have the potential to substitute a nucleotide for another at a unique positionintroducing a point mutation without causing DSBs or requiring any exogenous DNA [43][44][45]. Cytosine base editors (CBEs) are used to create C-to-T edits while adenosine base editors (ABEs) can create A-to-G substitutions [43,44]. While these technologies have been widely applied from agriculture to human therapy [43,46,47], they remain under-explored in insects which could serve as excellent options for the development of targeted genetic intervention strategies and genetic biocontrol [48]. For example, they could be used to introduce and spread pesticide resistance [49] or heat tolerance allele [50] in various insect species. e organism D. melanogaster is however used as a model to study the transgenic expression of CBEs and ABEs while targeting the germlines. In a study by akkar et al., the white gene was targeted using first generation CBEs and ABEs and an average germline editing rate of 70% was reported [51]. In another study by Doll and colleagues, an evolved version of the Rattus norvegicus APO-BEC1 (CBE evoAPOBEC1 ) and Petromyzon marinus cytidine deaminase 1 (CDA1) protein (CBE evoCDA1 ) were evaluated, they reported a germline transmission rate of ~ 99% efficiency when using CBE evoCDA1 while the CBE evoAPOBEC1 showed lower base editing rates (70-95%) [52]. Unfortunately, both studies utilized an elevated temperature of 28-29 °C to achieve higher editing rates in specific situations, making it non ideal for the survival of the Drosophila which requires temperatures of 25 °C [53,54]. In a 2024 study by Clark et al. [55], the efficiency of three different CBEs at 25 °C were investigated: (i) the original Rattus norvegicus-derived cytosine deaminase APOBEC1 (rAPO-1) [32], (ii) the AID*Δ variant of the human AID cytidine deaminase(AID*Δ) [56], and (iii) an optimized version of the original APOBEC1 (ancBE4) [57]. eir study reported an editing efficiency of >99% when the ubiquitous actin promoter was used at 25 °C. A wider editing window was also reported for AID*Δ compared to the others -signifying its potential for introducing multiple mutations at a target site. In addition, by targeting the β-Tubulin (β-Tub) and sex-lethal (sxl) genes, the base editors are able to cause male sterility and female lethality, respectively. is highly efficient CBEs, though precise, formed increased indel when transmitted maternally. us, through these studies using fruit flies, the CBE repertoire alongside the fine workings of base editors are constantly being characterized and elucidated.

div.head: The future of Drosophila in precision cancer medicine and drug development
div.p: Like other disease research, oncological research relies heavily on reliable and representative models. ese models include cancer cell lines, 3D model organoids and organisms such as Drosophila melanogaster, zebrafish, and genetically engineered mouse model, pigs, patient-derived xenografts (PDXs), and computational cancer models [58]. All cancer models aim to mimic some features of human cancer cells, however, due to the heterogeneous nature of these tumors, finding the most fitting model which can best reflect the tumor system has remained a challenge [59][60][61]. Figure 1 is a summary and flowchart of the various models used currently in oncological research. ese models form the basis used to investigate the pathological, biochemical, and genetic pathways of cancer cells.

Drosophila melanogaster has greatly contributed to the understanding of the molecular basis of cancer biology by unveiling the mechanism of action of various cancer proteins. Ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) is used in the induction of mutation in D. melanogaster larva to form cancerous models. e tumorous tissue resides in the outer proliferative center (OPC) and central brain (CB) regions of the larva brain. e larval brain is then transplanted into the abdomens of adult female flies, where the tissue continues to proliferate. After several days, the host's ovaries are dissected and analyzed using immunofluorescence to detect labeled tumor cells that have metastasized. Engineered Drosophila melanogaster strains are crucial in therapeutic drug discovery and serve as effective platforms for drug screening. e precision and speed achieved with Drosophila in genomic research and functional assays surpass those of traditional mammalian cancer models. is model organism offers valuable insights into processes such as asymmetric cell division, metabolic changes, genome instability, centrosome abnormalities, and aberrant gene expression-all of which contribute to tumor initiation and cancer progression. e Drosophila genome shares significant homology with the human genome, with over 50% of human cancer-related proteins having orthologs in the fly. Notably, it has been instrumental in identifying cell polarity mutants and linking them to human tumor development [62,63]. Despite its great use as a model, it shows some limitations. In mammals, malignant cells undergoing metastasis typically enter local blood or lymph vessels before forming secondary tumors and colonizing nearby tissues.

is process is challenging to model in Drosophila due to their rudimentary hematopoietic system and a lymphatic system that differs significantly from that of mammals. As a result, tumors induced in Drosophila generally exhibit a much lower metastatic potential compared to human tumors [30]. In a more advanced approach, intricate combinations of genetic alterations commonly found in various colorectal cancers are translated into fruit fly models that mirror the specific tumors seen in individual patients. By combining these genetic alterations, scientists can precisely replicate each patient's cancer situation. Using these models, novel combination therapies customized for each cancer type have been developed. is approach could serve as a future strategy to leverage Drosophila genetics for truly personalized drug screening aimed at targeting individual cancers.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Drosophila melanogaster has proven to be a versatile and powerful model for cancer research, offering a unique blend of genetic tractability, cost-effectiveness, and evolutionary conservation with human oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Its applications span from fundamental insights into tumorigenesis to high-throughput drug screening and the development of personalized cancer therapies. e advent of CRISPR technologies and other genetic tools has further enhanced its utility, allowing for precise modeling of patient-specific mutations and real-time analysis of therapeutic responses. However, critical limitations persist, including anatomical and physiological differences from humans, challenges in replicating the full metastatic cascade, and limitations in simulating the tumor microenvironment and systemic responses. While Drosophila cannot entirely replace mammalian models, its integration into multi-model cancer research pipelines-especially in early-stage discovery and drug validation-remains invaluable. Future advancements will likely focus on refining its capacity to mirror human tumor heterogeneity and resistance patterns, thereby solidifying its role in precision oncology and translational cancer research.
